introduction: Xenophon, Hellenica 2.4.38–43. Read this controlled course adaptation with the glosses, then revisit its source and historical setting on page three.

The settlement, return, sacrifice, and oath follow Hellenica 2.4.38–42. The δείκνυμι/ἵημι examples and interpretive questions are course composition. Section 43 describes a later killing of leaders at Eleusis and subsequent reconciliation; it is not the same event as the first return in 403 BCE.

paragraphs.greek: Οἱ ἐκ τοῦ Πειραιῶς καὶ οἱ ἐκ τοῦ ἄστεως ἐπολέμουν. Παυσανίας δὲ καὶ οἱ πρέσβεις περὶ διαλλαγῶν ἐπράττοντο. τέλος οἱ ἄνδρες ἐπαύσαντο μαχόμενοι.
Οἱ δὲ ἐκ τοῦ Πειραιῶς εἰς τὴν πόλιν ἀνέβησαν. τὰ ὅπλα εἶχον καὶ εἰς τὴν ἀκρόπολιν ἦλθον. ἐκεῖ τῇ Ἀθηνᾷ ἔθυσαν. εἶτα οἱ πολῖται ἐβουλεύοντο.
Οἱ πολῖται ὤμοσαν μὴ μνησικακήσειν. οὐκ ἀεὶ τὰ παλαιὰ κακὰ πρὸς τοὺς ἄλλους φέρειν ἔμελλον. χαλεπὸν δὲ τὸ ἔργον· οἱ γὰρ ἄνθρωποι πολλὰ ἔπαθον.

reading.translation:
The men from Piraeus and the men from the city had been fighting. Pausanias and the envoys negotiated reconciliation. At last the men stopped fighting.

The men from Piraeus went up into the city. They had their arms and came to the Acropolis. There they sacrificed to Athena. Then the citizens deliberated.

The citizens swore not to bear grudges. They were not going to keep bringing old wrongs against one another. But the task was difficult, for the people had suffered much.

In the teaching example the citizen points out the Acropolis. His friend sees the men going up. “These men are now ceasing to fight; but what will they do tomorrow?”

Another example: the man sends a missile, and his companion lets go of a stone. But refraining from throwing and harming involves a decision. Not every power immediately passes into action.

Xenophon later also writes about those at Eleusis: their generals died. Reconciliation was not easy. What, then, is the citizen’s self-control? To hold power and anger with judgment.

blocks.title: διαλλαγή: becoming reconciled
body: διαλλαγή names reconciliation or a settlement of differences. μνησικακέω means bear a grudge or remember wrongs against someone; the oath uses its future infinitive with a negative.

Reconciliation is an activity and a relationship, not merely a feeling of calm. In the final lesson, σωφροσύνη must be considered alongside judgment about power, injury, and the conditions for shared life.

sections.title: 1. δείκνυμι: showing evidence
body: δείκνυμι is a -νυμι verb: δείκνυμι, δείκνυς, δείκνυσι; δείκνυμεν, δείκνυτε, δεικνύασι. The infinitive is δεικνύναι. The stem outside the present system differs: future δείξω and aorist ἔδειξα.

The verb means “show” or “point out.” In historical interpretation, distinguish what the source shows from what a reconstruction imagines. A grammatical example about pointing at the Acropolis is not independent testimony.

sections.title: 2. ἵημι and ἀφίημι
body: ἵημι means “send, let go.” Its present forms are ἵημι, ἵης, ἵησι; ἵεμεν, ἵετε, ἱᾶσι. ἀφίημι adds the sense “let go from, release.” Its infinitive is ἀφιέναι, distinct from ἀφιστάναι, “make withdraw.”
Learn future ἥσω and aorist singular ἧκα, ἧκας, ἧκε; the aorist plural uses εἷμεν, εἷτε, εἷσαν. The aorist infinitive is εἷναι, distinct from εἶναι, “to be”: the breathing matters.

sections.title: 3. Participles that complete a verb
body: A supplementary participle completes a verb’s meaning rather than merely adding a circumstance. παύονται μαχόμενοι means “they stop fighting”; the participle agrees with the subject. With perception, ὁρᾷ τοὺς ἄνδρας ἀναβαίνοντας means “he sees the men going up”: the participle agrees with the accusative people perceived.

Distinguish a supplementary participle from an attributive participle with an article and from a genitive absolute. Ask what the main verb needs: stop doing what? see whom doing what? Extended indirect discourse is reserved for later lessons.

sections.title: Meet Xenophon’s Hellenica
body: The Hellenica narrates Greek affairs from the closing years of the Peloponnesian War into the fourth century BCE. It is political and military history, with speeches, choices, omissions, and judgments that invite scrutiny. It differs in purpose and scale from the Socratic dialogues and from the literary Cyrus narrative.

The seven books cover Greek affairs from 411 to 362 BCE, beginning where Thucydides’ unfinished history breaks off. They follow Athens’ defeat in the Peloponnesian War, oligarchy and democratic restoration, Spartan ascendancy, shifting alliances, and the rise of Thebes. The closing battle at Mantinea leaves uncertainty rather than a simple declaration that one city has permanently won.

Xenophon organizes political and military events through commanders, assemblies, negotiations, speeches, and judgments about conduct. His attention is selective, and his experience and sympathies shape the narrative. Ask what a speech tries to accomplish, whose actions receive explanation, and what a compressed transition leaves unclear. A historian’s ordering of events can be as significant as an explicit verdict.

Reading invitation: start with Book 2, chapter 3, on the Thirty, then follow chapter 4 through resistance and restoration. Compare the settlement with the later Eleusis episode instead of stopping at the hopeful return to Athens. Our module’s question has grown from control of appetite to restraint in civic life: what practices let former enemies inhabit one city? Read the complete work as a sequence of difficult choices, not a storehouse of uncomplicated moral examples.

Our passage, 2.4.38–43, concerns reconciliation after civil conflict at Athens. Keep its sequence clear: settlement and return in 403 BCE, sacrifice and renewed civic life, then a later episode involving Eleusis. Our supplementary-participle examples are teaching constructions, not additional testimony.

sections.title: Return with arms, then a shared city
body: The men from Piraeus return armed to the city and sacrifice to Athena on the Acropolis. A political settlement must become a way of living together after violence. Former opponents do not suddenly lose their memories.

The oath not to bear grudges concerns how old wrongs will be used in renewed civic relations. It is not a claim that nothing happened. The settlement’s restrictions and exceptions should not be reduced to the slogan “everyone forgot everything.”

sections.title: Do not crop out Eleusis
body: Section 43 reports a later confrontation: leaders from Eleusis are killed when they come for a conference, and further reconciliation follows through friends and relatives. This disturbing event limits any simple picture of an effortless, wholly peaceful restoration.

Chronology matters ethically as well as historically. If we merge the later killing into the first return, we misdescribe the sequence; if we omit it, we make reconciliation look easier and cleaner than Xenophon’s own account allows.

sections.title: A citizen’s restraint
body: Stage a discussion without reenacting violence. One speaker explains why a community needs rules against renewed retaliation; another asks how victims’ losses can be acknowledged. Require each to state a concern the other has correctly identified.

Then trace the module’s movement: governing appetite, recognizing bodily limits, managing power over others, and living with former opponents. Use a supplementary participle to describe stopping an action. Explain what constructive action must follow the stopping.
